description:
Wesam Saad develops his argument that the gift of prophecy has ceased, beginning with the tests established in the previous session. A prediction attributed to God must be accurate; repeated success does not excuse a failed claim. He then turns to Ephesians 2:19–21 and the church’s foundation of apostles and prophets. In his interpretation, their foundational role belongs to the church’s beginning rather than its continuing structure. The central argument concerns the completed biblical canon. Wesam describes God’s word as inspired, authoritative, infallible and free from error, and asks whether a claim that God has spoken today can be separated from those qualities.

He argues that accepting the completion of Scripture is inconsistent with claiming additional divine revelation of that kind. The practical discussion examines testimony about evangelism, private warnings and a call to ministry. Wesam distinguishes God’s sanctifying work and convictions shaped by Scripture from an infallible private message. He warns that waiting for a special inward signal can displace obedience to God’s already revealed will. A call to ministry is assessed through recognised giftedness, biblical character, desire to serve and the counsel of believers who know the person. Throughout, he urges listeners to define their terms and measure spiritual claims by the written word.

questions.question: Why does Wesam return to the accuracy of a claimed prophecy?
questions.answer: He applies Deuteronomy 18 consistently: a failed prediction cannot be excused by earlier successes or by learning to hear more accurately. He nevertheless says this test alone is not his full proof that the gift has ceased. It is the first step in the argument he develops.

questions.question: How does he use the foundation language in Ephesians 2?
questions.answer: Wesam reads apostles and prophets as foundational gifts belonging to the church’s beginning. He compares them with a foundation that is laid before the rest of a building is constructed. He also distinguishes being an eyewitness of the risen Christ from being appointed an apostle; witnessing alone is not sufficient in his account.

questions.question: What qualities does he identify with God’s written word?
questions.answer: He describes Scripture as inspired or breathed out by God, authoritative, infallible and entirely free from error. In the argument, these qualities follow from God being the one who speaks. They form the standard by which he examines claims that a person has received a further word from God.

questions.question: Why does he see a conflict between a completed canon and additional divine revelation?
questions.answer: Wesam argues that if God truly speaks a new message, it carries the authority and truthfulness of His speech. He therefore regards a claim to additional inspired, authoritative revelation as inconsistent with saying that the biblical canon is complete. This is the central theological inference he asks listeners to assess.

questions.question: How can waiting for a special inward signal hinder evangelism?
questions.answer: Wesam describes a believer waiting to feel that God has personally directed them to speak, even though Scripture already calls them to share the gospel. Since evangelism can feel uncomfortable, waiting for inward peace may become a reason never to act. He encourages obedience and giving God thanks for the result without claiming an extra revelation.

questions.question: Does his argument deny that God changes a believer’s desires or brings conviction?
questions.answer: Wesam expressly says he is not denying God’s sanctifying, changing and moulding work. His concern is how such experiences are described and tested. He distinguishes responding to the revealed moral will of God in Scripture from claiming to possess a new, authoritative message from God.

questions.question: How does Wesam explain a biblical call to ministry?
questions.answer: He points to recognised giftedness, the character qualifications described in Titus 1 and 1 Timothy 3, a desire to preach and shepherd, and the counsel of godly people who know the person’s life. In his account, the call is recognised through Scripture and the church’s assessment rather than an unexplained private experience.

questions.question: Does a private prediction appearing to come true settle whether God spoke?
questions.answer: Wesam says that fulfilment alone does not settle the claim. He directs the questioner back to the previous lesson’s tests and asks what they mean by saying God spoke. He insists that the claimed message must be examined against the authority and truthfulness attributed to God’s word, rather than accepted merely because an event occurred.
